angle: Edgar's free tokens were never built to attack: four payoffs turn every creature that enters into life gone at all three seats at once, and one two-mana Vampire is verified to be exactly lethal to a pod at twelve.

teases: One {B}{B} Vampire, one doubler, three payoffs — and a pod at twelve is dead
Your own Olivia's Wrath eats a converter, a doubler and the flying enabler
Never keep a hand for Edgar: median cast turn six, out by then in 52.3% of games
The end-step drain that leaves a 15-life opponent alive at exactly 1

departments.note: Hero is Edgar Markov's art_crop from the Innistrad Remastered printing in cards.json. The kicker states the finding from case 009 — nine triggers, no combat step — rather than a tier word. Coverline names the per-seat number, not the pod total: 12 each, 36 across the table, and the two are not interchangeable.
Five acts, promises verbatim from issue_spec. No extra furniture — the map must read in one glance.

departments.headline: THE ZONE IS THE ENGINE
departments.dek: Your commander costs six mana, and the best thing he does costs none of it. Read the tax ladder before you decide Edgar Markov is worth casting at all.
departments.body:
Which card do you always have? Not the one you drew — the one in the command zone. CR 903.6 puts Edgar Markov there face up before anybody has a hand, and that guarantee is the only one this format hands you.

Eminence is why it matters here. It reads “Whenever you cast another Vampire spell, if Edgar is in the command zone or on the battlefield, create a 1/1 black Vampire creature token.” An ability that states which zones it functions in functions only from those zones — CR 113.6b — and this one names the command zone out loud. Stack 002 confirms it firing from there.

So the engine is live on turn one and it costs nothing. Two riders travel with it. The tokens are created, not cast, so they never trigger eminence a second time. And casting Edgar is not casting another Vampire spell — he is the one Vampire in your deck that mints nothing.

Now price the man himself. Six, then eight, then ten, then twelve: CR 903.8 adds {2} for every previous command-zone cast, and that cost compounds for the rest of the game. The ladder beside this column is the whole argument for leaving him home.

Colour identity is why the 99 looks the way it does. CR 903.4 reads mana symbols in the cost and in the rules text, so {3}{R}{W}{B} buys white's exile and board-wide protection, black's tutors and drains, and red's damage payoffs. It also shuts the door on blue counterspells and green ramp: this deck answers a permanent after it resolves, or it does not answer it.

Is the 21-damage clock real? CR 903.10a ends a player dealt 21 combat damage by one commander, and Edgar is a 4/4 with first strike and haste who puts a +1/+1 counter on every Vampire he attacks alongside, himself included. Treat it as a coincidence you can cash. Commander damage points at one seat; this deck's kill points at three.

★ Coach's read. The table re-prices you the moment the card is read out, so stop buying anonymity you cannot afford. Spend the budget on order instead: land the two-mana payoffs while they still look like durdle, and let the six-mana commander arrive last, to a board he makes lethal rather than one he has to build.

★ And be honest about protection. Your engine does not route through Edgar — eminence keeps minting whatever happens to him — so insurance on him is insurance on the wrong thing. What his presence does buy is a discount: Flawless Maneuver costs {2}{W} while he waits in the zone and {0} the moment he is on the battlefield.

captions.Flawless Maneuver: **THE ZONE SETS THE PRICE:** {2}{W} while Edgar waits in the command zone, {0} the moment he is on the battlefield. Casting him is also a discount on protecting everything else you own.

pilot_tips.text: Cast Edgar for the attack trigger, never for the tokens — he is the one Vampire spell in your deck that mints nothing.

departments.pull_quote: The only card you always have is the one you never need to cast.
departments.note: Tax ladder and Commander File are renderer-computed from cards.json and goldfish_metrics.json: mean cast turn 6.639, out by turn six 52.3%. Coaching paragraphs are marked ★ in the body so the two voices stay separable on the page.

departments.headline: NOBODY HAS TO BLOCK
departments.dek: Every Vampire you cast is two bodies, and every body that enters costs all three opponents life at once. Build the layer that charges for it and the combat step becomes optional.

callouts.title: LAND THE UGLY TWO-DROP
callouts.text: Impact Tremors and Corpse Knight cost two and read as durdle. Play them into an empty board; one damage has never had a removal spell pointed at it.

callouts.title: DOUBLE THE EVENT, DON'T ADD TO IT
callouts.text: Anointed Procession, Mondrak, Glory Dominus and Elspeth, Storm Slayer replace the token creation rather than adding a token to it. Stack 002 has the arithmetic: one becomes two becomes four, and the order you pick cannot change the answer.

callouts.title: THEN CAST ANYTHING
callouts.text: With one doubler and three payoffs down, a {B}{B} Vampire is nine separate triggers and twelve damage at every seat — stack 009 counts it. The cheapest card in your hand is now the lethal one.

callouts.title: KEEP COMBAT AS THE BACKUP
callouts.text: A lord or anthem turns up in 83.2% of games at a mean turn of 2.60, so the alpha strike is always there. Take it after the entries have already done the work, not instead of them.

captions.Impact Tremors: **TWO MANA, ZERO RESPECT:** one damage to each opponent for every creature entering. It looks like nothing on turn two and it is the card that changes what your deck is.
captions.Anointed Procession: **REPLACEMENT, NOT ADDITION:** it does not hand you an extra token, it changes how many the effect makes — which is exactly why a second doubler multiplies instead of adding.
captions.Purphoros, God of the Forge: **THE BIG ONE:** 2 damage to each opponent per entry, on an indestructible permanent that usually is not even a creature. A creature sweeper does not touch him.

pilot_tips.text: Cast Corpse Knight early even though it is a Zombie and mints no token — it converts, and converting is the half you are short of.

departments.pull_quote: The cheapest card in your hand is the lethal one.

departments.headline: SIXTY-THREE SPELLS, ONE EVENT
departments.dek: Sorted by what each card does when a creature enters the battlefield, because that is the moment this deck is built around. The four converters lead; almost everything else exists to feed them.

roster.role: The conversion layer: every entry is damage
The multipliers: one token becomes four
Bodies that print bodies, for free
cards: Legion's Landing // Adanto, the First Fort

roster.role: Lords, anthems, and the counters that make them fly
The deterministic kill, and the rent it pays
cards: Vito, Thorn of the Dusk Rose

roster.role: Cheap Vampires that bank a token on the way down
Interaction, and insurance sized for a board
Fuel: draw, wishes, rebates and rocks

cards: Midgar, City of Mako // Reactor Raid

captions.Corpse Knight: **THE ODD ONE OUT:** a Zombie Knight, so casting it mints no eminence token and no lord ever pumps it. It causes life loss rather than damage — the exact wording Bloodletter of Aclazotz doubles.
captions.Olivia's Wrath: **READ YOUR OWN BOARD FIRST:** every non-Vampire creature shrinks by your Vampire count, and five of your thirty creatures are not Vampires. Cast it before you deploy Corpse Knight, Abzan Falconer, Mondrak and Ocelot Pride, never after.
captions.Cavern of Souls: **THE ONE RESTRICTED SOURCE:** name Vampire and your Vampire spells cannot be countered — but that coloured mana casts creature spells only. It cannot pay for Castle Locthwain's draw or Bloodline Keeper's flip.

pilot_tips.text: Pay Diabolic Intent's sacrifice with an eminence token and never with a lord — the token was free and the tutor is not.

departments.pull_quote: Thirty creatures, four ways to charge for them, and a machine no wrath can reach.
departments.note: Roster covers all 96 non-commander entries in eleven groups, load-bearing first; nothing falls through to the renderer's Depth bucket. Purphoros leads group one so the Featured Artist hero resolves to him. Counts to quote: 100 copies across 97 entries, 63 spells, 37 land copies, 30 creatures.

departments.headline: NEVER KEEP FOR EDGAR
departments.dek: You have just read the distribution — eight one-drops, seventeen two-drops, 37 lands. Now grade four openers against it, because the simulation keeps 81.8% of first sevens and the Coach ships one of them anyway.

hands.why: Three lands that can all arrive untapped, two one-mana Vampires worth two bodies each, a lord, and the two-mana payoff that turns the whole thing into damage. This is the shape the drill is looking for: something to cast on turn one, turn two and turn three, and a converter waiting behind it.

Two lands reads risky until you price the mana. Ancient Tomb into Sol Ring is three available on turn one against a simulated mean of 1.0, and Herald's Horn rebates {1} off every Vampire behind it. Both lands enter untapped, and that is the detail that saves the keep.

Half a deterministic kill and four five-drops. Two of those lands enter tapped no matter what you do, nothing happens before turn five, and your eminence dividend for four whole turns is zero. Ship anything whose cheapest spell costs four.

hands.verdict: SHIP — the hand the machine keeps
hands.why: The simulation's rule keeps any seven with two to five lands, so this five-lander passes it — and the Coach ships it anyway. One castable spell before turn four, and protection plus a tutor are luxuries in an opener rather than a plan. The badges disagreeing in public is the honest version of this section.

captions.Concealed Courtyard: **THE FIRST-THREE-TURNS LAND:** untapped exactly while eight one-drops and seventeen two-drops need it to be. Fifteen of the 37 lands can enter tapped; only three of them always do.
captions.Ancient Tomb: **TWO MANA FOR TWO LIFE:** the fastest land here, and your speed is worth the life. It is what turns a two-lander into a turn-two three-drop.
captions.Herald's Horn: **THE MARGINAL-HAND FIXER:** {1} off every Vampire spell and a free look at the top each upkeep. Ramp or fixing shows up in 67.7% of games at a mean turn of 2.98.

pilot_tips.text: Grade a one-drop by casts, not by stats — Vampire of the Dire Moon on turn one is a deathtouch blocker plus a banked token before it does anything else.

departments.pull_quote: He is face up in the command zone before your first decision. Mulligan as though he does not exist.

departments.headline: COMMIT BEFORE YOU READ ON
departments.dek: Two boards, two hard reads: a turn six where your commander is finally castable, and a turn seven where lethal costs one black mana and the control seat has sat on five lands for two turns. Pick your line, then check ours.

callouts.title: COUNT ENTRIES, NOT CARDS
callouts.text: One Vampire spell with a doubler down is three creature-entry events — two tokens and the body. Every converter on the battlefield reads each one separately.

callouts.title: PRICE THE COMMANDER HONESTLY
callouts.text: Six mana buys one attacker and a counter on each Vampire. The same six mana buys three cheap Vampires, six entries, and all the damage attached to them.

callouts.title: A KILL THAT COSTS ONE MANA IS NEVER WRONG
callouts.text: A converter that has already removed a seat is a card you cashed. A converter still sitting there when the wrath resolves is a card you paid for and never spent.

captions.Knight of the Ebon Legion: **ONE BLACK MANA, THREE ENTRIES:** with a doubler down, the cheapest Vampire in the deck is a token, a token and a body — and every converter counts all three.
captions.Mondrak, Glory Dominus: **THE SECOND BITE:** each replacement effect gets exactly one application, so two doublers take one token to four rather than to three (stack 002).
captions.Abzan Falconer: **COUNTERS BECOME EVASION:** every creature you control carrying a +1/+1 counter has flying, which is how a row of 1/1 tokens attacks a seat with two ground blockers.

pilot_tips.text: Drain first, then deploy — Socialite's extra counter applies only while an opponent has already lost life this turn.

departments.pull_quote: Six mana for one attacker, or six mana for six entries. It is not close.
departments.note: Both spreads come from decisions/*.json. Never reveal the recommendation above the branches — the renderer places it last, and the callouts above must teach the arithmetic without naming the call.

departments.headline: EXACTLY LETHAL, ZERO MARGIN
departments.dek: Seven case files, and the one that matters most is not an infinite. One {B}{B} Vampire, one doubler, three payoffs: nine triggers, twelve damage at every seat, and a pod at twelve is dead with no combat step anywhere in the sequence.

callouts.title: THE PRIMARY PLAN, ON THE RECORD
callouts.text: Stack 009 tests the deck's own world-view rather than its lottery ticket. Nine triggers, 12 damage per seat, 36 across the pod — and one trigger fewer leaves all three opponents standing at 1 or 2.

callouts.title: THE BOUND, AND WE LEAD WITH IT
callouts.text: Stack 007 is a refutation. Seven tapped creatures under Bloodletter of Aclazotz drain 14 apiece at your end step, and an opponent at 15 survives at exactly 1. That is reach, not a table kill, and the file says so.

callouts.title: THE TICKET YOU HAPPEN TO BE HOLDING
callouts.text: Stacks 004 and 006 are deterministic table-kills for zero mana. A complete pair is drawn in 4.6% of games, 2.6% by turn six — present it when a window opens, and never slow the board to protect it.

callouts.title: WHAT EVERY ITERATION COSTS YOU
callouts.text: Both loops hand the table a priority window, and Bloodthirsty Conqueror is a creature. Instant-speed creature removal breaks the chain at any iteration; the record names that price rather than hiding it.

captions.Warleader's Call: **THE PAYOFF THAT IMPROVES BOTH KILLS:** one damage to each opponent per entry, plus an anthem that makes your tokens 2/2. Stack 009 counts three of its triggers.
captions.Bloodletter of Aclazotz: **IT DOUBLES THEIRS, NEVER YOURS:** the clause replaces an opponent's life loss during your turn. Your own gain off the same trigger is untouched (stacks 003 and 007).
captions.Bloodthirsty Conqueror: **HONEST RENT:** a 5/5 flying deathtouch Vampire that pays full price on the nineteen games in twenty when the loop never happens.

departments.pull_quote: Nine triggers off a two-drop. One fewer and everybody lives.
departments.note: Seven presentable files render here: 002, 003, 004, 006, 007, 008, 009. Lead the reader on 009 (the primary plan) and 007 (the refutation), not on the infinites — they assemble in 4.6% of games and the issue must not read as a combo primer.

departments.headline: WHEN THEY START COUNTING YOU
departments.dek: You stop being a creature deck the first time a creature entering costs all three seats life. That moment is exact, it is cheap, and you get to choose when it arrives.

callouts.title: THREAT WINDOW: THE CONVERTER LANDS
callouts.text: Purphoros, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call or Corpse Knight resolving onto a board that already holds a doubler. A converter is in hand in 52.5% of games at a mean turn of 3.28; paired with a multiplier it is 40.2% at mean turn 4.53. Plan your archenemy turn for four or five, not for whenever Edgar shows up.

callouts.title: SAY WHAT THE WRATH COSTS YOU
callouts.text: Your machine is enchantments and a command-zone trigger. Their sweeper is a bad trade against you and a fine one against the seat to your left — pointing that out is free, and it is true, which is the only table talk that keeps working.

callouts.title: THE SEAT THAT CAN ACTUALLY BEAT YOU
callouts.text: Broad exile and enchantment removal, not the wrath. Despark and Anguished Unmaking put one answer in hand in 30.8% of games and 23.8% by turn six, so hold them for the permanent that ends your function rather than the one that looks scary.

captions.Elspeth, Storm Slayer: **LAST PIECE DOWN, NEVER FIRST:** a five-mana planeswalker gets attacked on sight. Deploy her onto a board that converts immediately, or leave her in hand.
captions.Teferi's Protection: **ONE CARD, TWO PROBLEMS:** it answers the sweeper and the swing-back together. A protection piece is held in 68.1% of games, 56.7% by turn six.
captions.Charismatic Conqueror: **IT TAXES THEIR TURN:** every untapped artifact or creature an opponent plays either arrives tapped or hands you a lifelink Vampire. Tokens made on their turn, converted on yours.

pilot_tips.text: Land Impact Tremors on turn two into an empty board — one damage reads as durdle, and nobody has ever spent removal on it.

departments.pull_quote: Sequence the boring cards first. The scary ones are cheaper when nobody is holding an answer.

departments.headline: WHO ACTUALLY BEATS YOU
departments.dek: Not the sweeper, and certainly not the graveyard hate. Find the seat holding broad exile, because that is the only player at the table who can switch the machine off.

threats.read: The wrath is a worse card against you than against anyone else at the table, and the whole matchup is built on that. Anointed Procession, Impact Tremors, Warleader's Call, Cathars' Crusade, Caretaker's Talent, Patchwork Banner, Herald's Horn, Legion's Landing and Elspeth all live through it, Purphoros is indestructible and usually not even a creature, and eminence rebuilds at a token per Vampire cast with nothing spent. One caveat: Corpse Knight is a creature, so every wrath trims your conversion layer by one. The toughness-based sweeper hurts more than the destroy-based one, and Cathars' Crusade counters are the answer to it.

Structurally your best matchup, for a reason worth knowing cold: eminence is a triggered ability from the command zone, not a cast, so a Sphere taxes the Vampire spell and never touches the token it mints. Eight one-drops and seventeen two-drops keep paying under the tax, and two cost reducers lower the bill rather than raising your sources. Leave Edgar zoned longest here — six mana is the first thing a tax prices out, and the engine has been running since turn one anyway.

Re-ask the role and take the other seat: against a faster board you are the control, and you can be without changing a card. Lifelink tokens from Charismatic Conqueror, Legion's Landing and Mavren Fein, deathtouch from Vampire of the Dire Moon and Preacher of the Schism, first strike from Stromkirk Captain and Cemetery Gatekeeper. A wide board turns their small creatures into dead cards without you drawing anything. Sweep carefully — Olivia's Wrath is asymmetric only to the extent you stay on type.

You are the clock and you are fast enough to be one: a lord or anthem at a mean turn of 2.60, a multiplier at 2.68, a converter at 3.28. Held answers rot, so spend the exile on the piece that ends the game rather than the piece that looks scary. Present the plan that survives being answered — a removed multiplier costs a card, an interrupted alpha strike costs the board. Do not steer toward the loop here: it is complete in 4.6% of games and one instant-speed removal spell breaks it at any iteration.

This one is close to free and you should encourage it. There is no graveyard plan to attack — the kills are creature entries, attack triggers and a lifegain loop, and every payoff sits on the battlefield as a permanent. A Rest in Peace effect costs the reanimator seat their whole deck and costs you one Cemetery Gatekeeper trigger and a channel from Takenuma. Say yes to that trade every time and help the hate resolve.

pilot_tips.text: Aim Despark at the tax piece rather than the trophy — it exiles mana value 4 or greater, so the cheap prison enchantment is exactly what it cannot touch.

departments.pull_quote: Help the graveyard hate resolve. It costs you one trigger and costs them a deck.
departments.note: Threat meters are editorial reads, not measured rates — they order the matchups by how much the archetype actually threatens this deck. Every named out is a card in the 99.

departments.headline: FOUR TUTORS, ONE DEFAULT ANSWER
departments.dek: Three blank cheques and one Vampire-only search that leaves a body behind. Your default wish is a converter — stop agonising over it and go get one.

captions.Demonic Tutor: **THE ONLY WISH YOU CAN CAST BEHIND:** two mana plus a two-drop is a real turn four at 4.005 mean available mana. Anything dearer means you are buying next turn — say so before you cast it, not after.
captions.Forerunner of the Legion: **A BODY AND A SEARCH:** {2}{W} for a 2/2 Vampire Knight, an eminence token, and any Vampire put on top of your library. It spends your next draw, so cast it on a turn you wanted a body anyway.
captions.Vampiric Tutor: **CAST IT ON THEIR END STEP:** one mana, any card on top, one draw surrendered. Do it the turn before yours and the card is in hand when you untap.

pilot_tips.text: Ask which missing piece turns your board into damage this turn — never which card in the deck is best.

departments.pull_quote: Tutor the irreplaceable. Stack the classes you want every game.

departments.headline: BLACK IS THE ONE THAT BINDS
departments.dek: Black carries 49.4% of this deck's coloured pips on 41.8% of its coloured sources, and it is the colour of the one-drops. You are best supported in the colour you need least.

captions.Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth: **ONE CARD, ONE FIX:** every land you control becomes a Swamp, which repairs the shortest colour in the deck. Sequence it early whenever the hand is black-hungry.
captions.Patchwork Banner: **THE ROCK THAT IS ALSO A LORD:** name Vampire and it pumps the team while tapping for any colour. Five rocks lift black from 23 land sources to 26 in total, and 66.7% on curve to 74.2%.
captions.Nomad Outpost: **ONE OF ONLY THREE:** fifteen of the 37 lands can enter tapped, but only Nomad Outpost, Savai Triome and Midgar, City of Mako do it unconditionally. Everything else has a price you can choose to pay.

pilot_tips.text: Never plan an activated ability around Cavern of Souls — its coloured mana casts creature spells only, and an ability is not a spell.

departments.pull_quote: A yardstick asking for 36 black sources inside a 37-land deck is arithmetic that does not exist.
departments.note: Quote lands.total (37), never lands.entries (34). The yardstick column is a yardstick and the prose must say what the gap costs — sequencing posture, not a shopping list. The declared art break follows this section.

departments.headline: WHAT TO ACTUALLY EXPECT
departments.dek: Ten thousand seeded games with no opponents and no removal in them. The figure that decides this deck is 52.5% — how often a card that turns an entry into damage is in your hand at all.

callouts.title: THE HALF THAT BINDS
callouts.text: TOKEN → DAMAGE is drawn in 52.5% of games, 42.3% by turn six, mean turn 3.28. A multiplier turns up in 78.2% at mean turn 2.68. The bodies are never the shortage — the charge for them is.

callouts.title: THE JOINT NUMBER
callouts.text: A converter and a multiplier together — the go-wide kill — is 40.2% assembled and 27.5% by turn six, mean turn 4.53. That is your archenemy turn, and it lands on four or five.

callouts.title: THE ONE TO STOP WAITING FOR
callouts.text: Edgar's mean cast is turn 6.639 and his median is six, with 52.3% of games having him out by then. Every plan that begins “once Edgar lands” actually begins on turn seven.

callouts.title: WHAT A SIMULATION IS NOT
callouts.text: No opponents, no removal, no blockers, no combat. These are resource-development rates and not win rates, and the assumptions box says so every issue because it is the only honest way to print them.

captions.Sol Ring: **THE ONE-CARD TURN:** mean available mana is 2.141 on turn two and 3.168 on turn three. Sol Ring moves you a whole row up that table.
captions.Night's Whisper: **THE ONLY DRAW THAT NEEDS NO BOARD:** a draw engine turns up in 60.3% of games, and four of the five want creatures on the table first. This one does not.
captions.Twilight Prophet: **TEN PERMANENTS:** the condition reads as demanding until you count tokens — mean bodies is 4.103 by turn six and 6.593 by turn ten.

departments.pull_quote: One game in twenty is a ticket. Fifty-two in a hundred is a plan.
departments.note: Cite figures exactly as goldfish_metrics.json reports them. 52.5% and 40.2% are assembled-by-turn-10 rates; 42.3%, 27.5% and 23.8% are by-turn-six. Never blend the two in one sentence.

departments.headline: BUY THE RATE, NOT THE CEILING
departments.dek: Ten cards, ranked, and three of them do the single thing this deck is short of. Five copies of an effect is 31% of opening sevens, seven copies is 41%, ten is 54% — that is what a slot actually purchases.

callouts.title: WHERE THE SLOT GOES
callouts.text: Four cards convert an entry into each-opponent damage, and that class is in hand in 52.5% of games — 25.8% of opening sevens. Another rung on that ladder moves the number you see every game rather than the ceiling you see occasionally.

callouts.title: THE SECOND THIN CLASS
callouts.text: An answer to a noncreature permanent is two cards: 30.8% assembled, 23.8% by turn six, 13.7% of opening sevens. Against three opponents that is the axis that binds second, and it is cheap to widen.

callouts.title: WHAT NOT TO BUY
callouts.text: Not a third copy of a two-card kill you draw one game in twenty, and not a fourth doubler — the multiplier half of this deck is finished at 78.2%. And not a bracket: the floor is 4 on four Game Changers, and nothing on this list moves it.

captions.Kalitas, Traitor of Ghet: **THE NAMED CUT:** a genuinely good card that converts no entry into damage, which is the only currency this list trades in. That is what makes it the slot the top pick asks for.
captions.Sanguine Bond: **FIVE MANA, NO BODY, NO TYPE:** the one slot the token plan genuinely subsidises. The list would trade it for a drain that arrives attached to a Vampire.
captions.Sunbaked Canyon: **THE COLOUR ARITHMETIC:** red gets 17 sources for eleven cards that never ask for more than one red pip. Black gets 26 for 28 cards that routinely ask for two.

departments.pull_quote: Redundancy is a rate you can buy. Power is a ceiling you can only hope for.
departments.note: Exactly ten entries render from considering.json, each chipped In the box or Scouted. Every recommendation is ★; the counts and rates beside them are ◆. A line one of the ten would open stays a candidate until a stack passes.

departments.headline: READ THEM TWICE
departments.dek: Seven files, every citation verbatim, including the one that concludes the line does not kill the table. The refutation is filed on exactly the same terms as the kills, which is the entire point of keeping a record.
departments.pull_quote: A record that only holds the wins is not a record.
departments.note: Renderer generates every case from checker-passed artifacts; no summarising, no truncation. Seven files are presentable: 002, 003, 004, 006, 007, 008, 009. Case A-009 cleared in three review cycles and A-003 in two — print the iteration counts, they are part of the story.

departments.headline: NOBODY PAINTED THIS DECK
departments.dek: Ninety-two artists split 126 cards and the two leaders hold four apiece. There is no house style in this collection — so the feature goes to the hand that painted the card the issue's centrepiece rests on.

featured.note:
Two cards out of 126, and one of them is the whole thesis. Eric Deschamps painted Purphoros, God of the Forge — the god who turns a creature entering the battlefield into 2 damage at every seat, and the card stacks 008 and 009 count trigger by trigger. He also painted Captivating Vampire, the lord that taps five Vampires and takes something of theirs.

Two of 126 is not dominance and we are not calling it that. The census reads as breadth and the numbers say so plainly: 92 artists, 126 cards counted, 131 copies, and the leaders holding four cards each. Fifty-nine sets contribute, and the largest single one gives eleven cards by eleven different artists.

The analysis found no contiguous collector-number runs anywhere in the collection. Nobody bought this deck whole. It was assembled a card at a time across a decade of printings, and a credits page with ninety-two names on it is exactly what that looks like.

also_worth_noting.note: A joint leader at four cards and no theme at all: Arcane Signet and Diabolic Intent sleeved, Akroma's Memorial and Leering Onlooker in the box.
The other leader at four, three of them lands — Castle Locthwain, Luxury Suite, Savai Triome. The fourth is Throne of the God-Pharaoh, the end-step drain case A-007 bounded.

Three entries but two cards: Strefan, Maurer Progenitor is counted twice because two printings are counted separately, and Vampire Gourmand is the third. The count is honest about printings, and we are honest about the count.
Three cards and four copies, one of them Mondrak, Glory Dominus — the second doubler whose arithmetic case A-002 settled.
Three cards, all of them night scenes — Blood Crypt, Silent Clearing, Twilight Prophet. The closest this collection comes to a mood board.
Two lands doing quiet jobs: Cavern of Souls, which makes your Vampire spells uncounterable, and Reflecting Pool.

captions.Captivating Vampire: **THE OTHER DESCHAMPS:** a lord whose second ability is a removal spell you already paid for — tap five untapped Vampires and take their best creature.
captions.Throne of the God-Pharaoh: **THE MANABASE'S HOUSE PAINTER, OFF DUTY:** Titus Lunter has four cards here and three are lands. This is the fourth, and it is the one the checker bounded.
captions.Twilight Prophet: **THREE FOR THREE:** every Seb McKinnon card in this deck is a nocturne, and this one drains the table at your upkeep once you control ten permanents.

departments.pull_quote: We count cards, not copies. Four Swamps are one credit.
departments.note: artist-credits reports standout: null — the lead artists hold four cards and its own note says to tell a breadth story, so the feature is an editorial pick and every count is recomputed by the renderer. rhythm_notes: Act I opens on the commander, so The Command Zone is the reader's first contact with the deck and its body copy introduces the engine before it teaches the format — tax ladder and colour identity land after the reader knows what eminence does. The Game Plan is the high narrative beat, and The 99 is the deliberate browsing trough after it. Act II is practice → participation → peak: Keep or Ship now reads after the roster, so its openers are graded against a distribution the reader has already seen, and the two SHIP verdicts name cards from groups they just browsed. The Kill closes the act as the payoff, and it is the issue's biggest layout. Act III is three consecutive Coach sections and reads as one continuous voice: reflection (Table Manners), reference (Know Your Enemy), instruction (Fetch Quests) — no two dense modes adjacent. Act IV is three consecutive Ledger sections and contains the only genuine dense adjacency in the book, Sources Say into By the Numbers; the renderer's declared full-bleed art break sits between them, and The Short List (imagination) closes the act on a light note. Act V drops to opt-in reference, then appreciation, then closure. Judge's Desk did not move: a claim still goes to the back of the book to be checked.
